headline: Fund-critical upgrade, registry, minting and pause surfaces are visible on-chain, but the exact uncontested governance/multisig execution path and signer thresholds were not fully recoverable.

findings.text: NXMaster is an OwnedUpgradeabilityProxy whose proxyOwner is TemporaryGovernance at 0x4A5C681dDC32acC6ccA51ac17e9d461e6be87900; another pinned proxy at 0x84edffa16bb0b9ab1163abb0a13ff0744c11272f is owned by NXMaster.

Multiple core/control contracts are upgradeable proxies: NXMaster, TemporaryGovernance, Registry, TokenController and the pinned proxy surfaces expose upgradeTo, transferProxyOwnership or upgradeContract-style functions; NXM token docs separately describe the NXM token as immutable, so upgradeability is mixed rather than uniformly immutable.

Official governance docs describe an optimistic path with an Advisory Board-created default outcome, 3-day vote period, 15% NXM supply quorum for rejection and a 24-hour timelock, but this run did not re-read those constants from the current governance contracts.

TemporaryGovernance exposes advisoryBoardMultisig = 0x51ad1265C8702c9e96Ea61Fe4088C2e22eD4418e and Registry reports ADVISORY_BOARD_SEATS = 5; docs list five Advisory Board members and describe an Emergency Pause Safe, but Safe threshold/owners were not obtained.

Governance docs state NXM holders can reject Advisory Board proposals using Snapshot with 15% total NXM supply quorum, 3-day voting and 24-hour timelock; these numbers are documentation evidence only in this run.

Emergency powers exist: docs say the Advisory Board or Emergency Pause Safe can pause RAMM or the entire protocol, and Registry exposes setEmergencyAdmin, proposePauseConfig, confirmPauseConfig, getPauseConfig and getSystemPause.

Worst visible power tier is T1 fund-critical if the governance/registry/proxy path can execute it: Registry exposes upgradeContract, TemporaryGovernance exposes execute, proxies expose upgradeTo, TokenController exposes mint/withdrawNXM, and Pool surfaces show claim-payout and asset-transfer functions. The actor and time-bound for the shortest executable path were not proven.

rationale.verdict: Assessment blocked because the run found T1-capable upgrade and fund-control surfaces, but did not establish the full shortest execution path, Safe thresholds/owners, and on-chain voting/timelock constants needed to distinguish orange from green or red.

protocol_metadata.about: Nexus Mutual is an Ethereum mutual where members buy cover for smart-contract, custody, slashing and depeg risks, stake NXM to underwrite products, and assess claims. The Capital Pool holds the assets backing NXM, receives cover premiums, pays accepted claims, and supports NXM minting or selling subject to mutual capital rules. V2-style modules include the Pool, Registry, TokenController, staking pools, cover products, RAMM and swap infrastructure.

headline: User-facing exits and claim/stake withdrawal functions are visible, but pause scope, pause caps and finalized-claim behavior were not recovered strongly enough to grade exit safety.

findings.text: Observed exit/exit-adjacent functions include TokenController.withdrawNXM, TokenController.withdrawNXMStakeAndRewards, Pool1.sellNXMTokens, Claims.submitClaim, Claims.submitClaimForMember and StakingPool withdrawals after stake-tranche expiration described in docs.

Access controls are not uniform: cover purchase and claim submission require Nexus Mutual membership per official user-flow docs, TokenController ABI includes OnlyMember/OnlyAdvisoryBoard-style errors, and Registry exposes isPaused(uint256).

Pause machinery is visible through Registry getPauseConfig = 0, getSystemPause config = 0, setEmergencyAdmin, proposePauseConfig and confirmPauseConfig, but the current role holders, pause bit meanings and maximum pause duration were not decoded.

Docs distinguish emergency pause powers from ordinary governance: Advisory Board or Emergency Pause Safe can pause RAMM or the entire protocol, but the fetched sources did not establish an auto-expiry or a governance-only indefinite pause path.

Queued or delayed flows exist: docs state claims review is typically 7 days, NXM selling is subject to capital conditions, and staking withdrawals happen after tranche expiration; exact hard maximums/caps for all exit paths were not recovered.
No permissionless forced-exit or escape-hatch mechanism for adversarial-admin scenarios was found in the fetched sources.

Exit and claim functions are exposed on-chain in fetched ABIs and the public SDK exists, so at least some exits are directly callable without the official frontend, subject to membership and protocol-state constraints.

rationale.verdict: Assessment blocked because the run could enumerate several exit functions but could not prove whether claims of finalized payouts or NXM/stake withdrawals can be paused indefinitely, which is the decisive red/orange/green boundary for this slice.

headline: Impacted TVS unclear: Nexus Mutual has visible oracle, RAMM/SwapOperator, investment, API and governance-mutable module surfaces, but the live external-dependency graph and fallbacks were not reconstructed.

findings.text: External-call surfaces are strongly suggested but not fully enumerated: Pool docs state swaps use RAMM/SwapOperator, the audit index lists USD Price Feed Oracle audits, TokenController links to Pool/Registry/StakingNFT/StakingPoolFactory, and Capital Pool docs describe ETH/USDC/cbBTC plus investments.

Human/committee processes feed into protocol outcomes: governance docs describe Advisory Board proposal defaults and member rejection votes, while cover flow docs describe claim review after IndividualClaims.submitClaim; exact committee/off-chain reporter powers into contracts were not fully read.
No material current bridge or cross-chain messaging dependency was verified in this run; the pinned protocol context and fetched docs are Ethereum-focused.

The protocol sells cover for third-party risks such as smart-contract hacks, custody failure, slashing and depegs, and capital-pool docs list cbBTC alongside ETH and USDC; this run did not identify user collateral receipt chains inside the mutual analogous to LRT/restaking collateral.

Fallback/circuit-breaker evidence is incomplete: Registry has system-pause and pause-config machinery, and docs describe emergency pause powers, but no live oracle fallback, investment-loss backstop or dependency-specific circuit breaker was verified on-chain.
No appchain, protocol-owned sequencer or DA layer was identified; the deployment examined is Ethereum mainnet, so L1 consensus is substrate rather than an autonomy dependency.

The Cover Router API is used to compute quote and pool-allocation inputs before Cover.buyCover, while claim review/voting is a workflow dependency; the run did not prove that any single off-chain operator must approve admission or settlement.

Governance-mutable dependency surface exists in principle: Registry exposes addContract, deployContract, removeContract, setKycAuthAddress and upgradeContract, but the exact timelock/exit window for adding or swapping externally trusted modules was not proven.

rationale.verdict: Assessment blocked because A1 and A6 remain incomplete: the run found credible dependency surfaces, but not the live oracle/investment/swap dependency addresses, their current fallback status, or the fraction of TVS impacted by a worst single dependency failure.

headline: Core write access is contract-gated by Nexus Mutual membership/KYC/whitelist mechanics even though SDK/direct-call paths exist.

findings.text: Core user entry points are membership-gated: official cover-buyer docs state users must be Nexus Mutual members before purchasing cover or making a claim and that transactions fail otherwise; Registry exposes join, isMember and getKycAuthAddress; TokenController/NXM surfaces expose whitelist functions.

No single privileged relayer was shown to approve every user action: the Cover Router API computes quote/pool-allocation inputs, but docs then have the user call Cover.buyCover and the public SDK gives developers an alternate interaction path.

Official Terms are context only: the fetched PDF says app/site availability may be interrupted, suspended or restricted and users must comply with applicable laws; no verbatim sanctions or jurisdiction-specific exclusion clause was extracted.
Independent access paths exist through the published @nexusmutual/sdk and public smart-contract repository, so the protocol is not captured solely by the official web UI.
No OFAC/sanctions oracle was observed in the assessed ABIs, but contract-level membership, KYC-auth and whitelist surfaces are explicit.

Read access is public through on-chain surfacers/ABIs, but write access for core cover/claim membership flows is gated to members; TokenController also controls NXM whitelist and membership-related token operations.

Fetched Terms clause evidence: app/site access can be interrupted, suspended or restricted, smart-contract use is at the user's own risk, and users must comply with applicable domestic and international laws.

steelman.red: The red case is strongest because buying cover and submitting claims, the core user actions, require Nexus Mutual membership and the contracts expose KYC-auth, membership and whitelist machinery.
steelman.orange: The orange case is that the contracts and SDK are publicly reachable, so the official publisher does not monopolize access, but admission still depends on a governance/member/KYC-controlled membership layer.
steelman.green: The green case is limited to members: once admitted, users can use SDK/direct contract paths rather than the official frontend.

rationale.verdict: Choosing red because the decisive grade input is contract-level admission, not frontend availability: official docs say non-members cannot buy cover or make claims, and fetched contract surfaces show Registry membership/KYC-auth plus TokenController/NXM whitelist controls.

headline: Major assessed contracts are explorer-verified and public repos/audits exist, but deployed-source-to-audited-commit correspondence and post-audit drift were not pinned.

findings.text: Representative pinned contracts and crawled current modules report ABI source etherscan or sourcify, including Pool1, NXMaster proxy, a pinned proxy, LegacyMemberRoles, TemporaryGovernance, Registry and TokenController.

A public NexusMutual/smart-contracts repository exists with contracts/deployments/docs folders and a public SDK repository exists, but this run did not pin a commit SHA or independently match deployed bytecode to repo source.

The official audits page lists a long audit history, including iosiro reports through March 2025, November 2024 USD Price Feed Oracle audits, 2022-2023 V2 module audits, a Chaos Labs economic audit, G0 Group reports and Solidified 2019 reports.

The firms fetched from the audit index are iosiro, Chaos Labs, G0 Group and Solidified; no fetched report from the commonly recognized Solidity-audit firm list was identified for a green-grade claim in this run.

Visible release metadata on the smart-contracts repo shows v3.4.0 on April 16, 2026, while the latest audit index entry fetched is March 2025; this run did not sample diffs to determine whether drift is material or re-audited.

Several proxies expose implementation addresses on the surfacers, including NXMaster, TemporaryGovernance, Registry and TokenController; implementation verification for every current fund-custody/settlement implementation was not fully checked separately.

steelman.red: The red case would require unverified bytecode, no repo or no audits, but the fetched surfacers show verified ABI sources and the official repo/audit pages exist.
steelman.orange: The orange case is strongest because verification and audits exist, but current deployment-to-repo/audited-commit correspondence and material post-audit drift were not established.
steelman.green: The green case is that the main assessed contracts are explorer-verified, the source repository is public, and there is a long audit history including recent 2024-2025 entries.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because the evidence is comfortably above red but below green: explorer/source verification, public repo and audits are present, yet no commit-pinned source match or material-drift review was completed for the current deployed implementations.
